strengths: The paper pairs the proposed regularizer with a solid theoretical analysis of the smoothness of the resulting loss function, which justifies its use as an additional term to the (W)GAN loss.
Experimental results show that the proposed regularizer provides a significant advantage in training GANs, especially for self-supervised tasks.

Although the paper is theoretically dense, it can still be followed by non-experts in the PH fields. Nevertheless, it would be helpful to remark the purpose of each theorem, or sequence of theorems, before introducing them.

The work mixes results from different ideas (mix of MMD, persistence measures, etc.), and may be useful beyond the scope covered by this paper (improving GAN training). It showcases the use of PPM which are interesting objects in their own, introduce novel possibly useful metric between these topological descriptors, etc.
Interesting experiments, mixing pedagogical Proof-of-Concept and more advanced experiments.
Nice animation in the supplementary material!
In general it is great to see a push towards scalable topological methods and this entails the core strengths of the paper, as it an impactful and relevant problem to work on.

Often in TDA, the focal point lies in theoretical justification of the methods with only limited empirical evidence, mostly on small datasets. Lack of scalability of PH being the main driver of this phenomenon and therefore this paper is of importance in building the bridge in applying TDA in large scale applications.

The theoretical justification is both thorough and sound and adopts a novel view on using PH in machine learning applications with the empirical evidence showing good improvements when using the regularization term.
weaknesses: The main weakness of the paper is the introduction and motivation of the problem and the relation of the proposed method to the current literature. From the introduction (and also the title), it isn’t really clear what problem the paper is going to tackle.

While the introduction talks about general regularizers for latent space representations, most of the methodological development and the experimental section tackle specifically the problem of regularizing GANs. I would be clearer about this from the beginning of the paper or show applications beyond GANs (beyond the shape-matching toy example).

I would also better frame the work in the context of GANs, and regularization strategies for GANs. A few methods are mentioned in the literature, but none is discussed in depth. For instance, PHom-GeM seems to share objectives and strategies similar to those of the proposed work. It would be ideal to compare also with some of these methods.

Also, it is not clear what theorems are novel, and which ones are just reported or adapted from results in the existing literature. Maybe they are all novel, but specifying the current state of the literature and which gaps need to be filled (from a theoretical point of view) would help to better understand the contribution.

While well written, the introduction and section 2 somewhat fail to motivate the need to account for the geometry/topology when comparing distributions in the latent space; the paper does not adequately explain why standard distribution matching techniques are insufficient, and why incorporating topological information is necessary.

The argument against Wasserstein-like distances between topological descriptors based on gradient smoothness seems weak, and it is not clear that the non-smoothness of Wasserstein distance gradients would be a significant issue in the context of stochastic gradient descent.
One may argue that GANs tend to be outdated in comparison to more modern generative models (DDPM, etc.), which could limit the broader relevance of the work.

Where the theoretical contributions have good exposition, the implementation details are less thoroughly addressed; the paper lacks details on how the authors differ from previous work in computing persistent homology on the GPU.
The experimental section's optimization of point clouds is not particularly convincing.
The figure could be improved by showing how the final output has converged and in two dimensions.
It is unclear whether optimizing only a subset of the whole point cloud at a time leads to convergence to the reference point cloud.
Only the loss of the training set over the iterations is shown, with no independent set distance to quantify the results.
An argument why the non-zero convergence is correct is missing, since none of the loss functions converge to zero.
The experimental section heavily relies on the Cramer loss, and it would be helpful to justify why this loss metric and model are used, especially given its prior rejection at ICLR 2018.
The scope of the experiments is rather limited; a variety of datasets and models should be used to demonstrate that the regularization consistently improves scores across the board.
The paper lacks comparison with comparable work on topological regularizers for classification problems.
A comparison with previous work on persistent homology regarding computational performance and accuracy would be valuable.
A logical and convincing experimental suite would require implementing multiple reference GAN architectures with more standard metrics.
It would be beneficial to evaluate the regularization term on other tasks such as classification and regression.
The non-standard setup for the point cloud optimization experiment needs to be convincingly revised.
